source.title: Harry Potter is Still Here! Probing Knowledge Leakage in Targeted Unlearned Large Language Models via Automated Adversarial Prompting

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table text is flattened, but Table 3’s model and before/after columns are identifiable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial prompting can elicit Harry Potter knowledge from unlearned models, using an automated suffix attack and leakage-rate measure.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports leakage rates before and after LURK probing for WHP and Task Vector. Table A1 gives qualitative before/after completions, but its caption calls the intervention “LURK Fine-Tuning” while the method describes prompt-suffix optimization; those examples are not used as separate rows. Table 2’s forget-quality and utility results do not directly measure the recovery behavior in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Uses GCG-optimized adversarial prompt suffixes (prompting only, no weight changes) to elicit Harry Potter references from WHP- and Task-Vector-unlearned models. It reports leakage rates before and after probing (Table 3), which bears directly on version E. For TV on Llama3.1-8B it also bears on A, because the authors call that unlearning near-perfect by FQ gap and utility.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that unlearned models retain substantial Harry Potter knowledge exposed by adversarial suffixes, and that larger models are more susceptible. TV, despite better utility, is more vulnerable than WHP on larger models. They take this as evidence that methods conceal rather than forget. OPT-2.7B with TV shows 0% leakage, but its pretrained model is also at 0%, so the probe cannot detect anything there.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses WHP, Task Vector, Gradient Ascent, and NPO as unlearning methods, then evaluates leakage with its own GCG-based LURK adversarial suffix search. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation edits, or quantization.
record.method_sensitivity: Leakage after probing differs by model and unlearning method; the paper reports higher leakage for larger models and no detected leakage for OPT-2.7B with TV.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The evaluation is restricted to fictional Harry Potter content. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. The retained ICLM-7B model is used in general unlearning evaluation, but the reported probing table does not give its leakage rate. The authors note that the probe may fail to detect knowledge when the pretrained model performs poorly on the data.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Table 3 results left out. Table A1’s qualitative completions are not separately cataloged because its caption describes LURK fine-tuning, while the paper’s method describes suffix prompting, leaving the intervention unclear.

untested.parts: Near-chance accuracy on a QA or MCQ measure; only FQ gap and leakage rate are reported. GA and NPO are never probed.
Not tested; there is no activation ablation or mechanism analysis. 'Concealment' is inferred from prompting results only.
Only white-box optimized suffixes are tested. Ordinary rephrasing, other languages and in-context information are not tested, nor are the GA and NPO models.

missing.what: Pre-probe leakage of the pretrained target models (0.0, 32.7, 69.7, 54.6%), needed as the reference for how much knowledge is recovered
FQ gap and utility for WHP and TV per model (e.g., TV Llama3.1-8B FQ gap 0.0062; TV Llama2-13B FQ gap equal to the target), showing which models count as 'successfully unlearned' before the attack
GA and NPO are unlearned but not probed; the paper reports perplexity near infinity for them

record.verdict_notes: Leakage means at least one canonical HP reference in a completion, judged by GPT-4o-mini with an o3-mini check. The judge was validated on only 50 queries. No uncertainty is reported, and the target models were never probed, so probed-vs-unprobed comparisons are asymmetric. WHP/TV unlearning was weak on the larger models (substantial pre-probe leakage), so part of the 'recovery' is pre-existing leakage. Table A1's 'LURK Fine-Tuning' caption appears to be a mislabel for suffix prompting; its examples are qualitative only.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not directly establish that targeted-knowledge accuracy is near chance while general ability is retained, and then compare recovery with a model that never learned the knowledge.
No recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or internal-edit mechanism test is reported.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
Tests optimized adversarial suffix prompting, not ordinary rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.
No counter-method that resists the attacks is tested.

rows.subject: Llama2-13B
rows.note: Before and after LURK probing, respectively; the post-probing rate exceeds half of queries.
rows.check: Before unlearning, the target leaked 69.7%. The unlearned model already leaks 15.5% unprobed, so unlearning was incomplete before the attack.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B
rows.note: Before and after LURK probing, respectively; the post-probing rate exceeds half of queries.
rows.check: The target leaks 54.6% unprobed; the probed unlearned model leaks 67.3%. The comparison is asymmetric because the target was not probed. The unlearned model already leaks 22.7% unprobed.

rows.subject: OPT-2.7B
rows.note: The paper says this model’s pretrained version also has a 0% leakage rate, so the probing algorithm cannot detect knowledge when the pretrained model performs poorly on the data.
rows.check: The pretrained OPT-2.7B also leaks 0%, and the authors say the probe cannot detect knowledge here. A 0→0 result cannot show recovery, so this is not evidence of absence.

rows.subject: Llama2-7B
rows.note: Before and after LURK probing, respectively.
rows.check: Leakage of 4.0% after probing, against 32.7% for the pretrained target, is a small recovery.

rows.subject: Llama2-13B
rows.note: Before and after LURK probing, respectively. The discussion gives 79.68% and describes it as exceeding WHP’s 53.39%.
rows.check: The target leaks 69.7% unprobed, and TV on Llama2-13B already leaks 29.1% unprobed. Table 2 gives TV's FQ gap here (1.5506) as equal to the target's, so unlearning barely took effect.

relationships.condition: Llama2-13B and Llama3.1-8B, unlearned with WHP or TV
relationships.reason: Adversarial suffixes raise leakage to 53–85% of queries (r3, r4, r7, r8), near or above the pretrained target's unprobed leakage. However, these models already leaked 15–46% before probing.
relationships.display_finding: Leakage rises from 15–46% before probing to 53–85% under adversarial suffixes, approaching or exceeding the pretrained model's unprobed leakage.

relation.reason: The study measures leakage before and after adversarial probing on unlearned models.

tranche.reason: A different method (GCG-based LURK suffix search) on the same question: does prompting alone recover unlearned knowledge?

source_check.notes: OPT-2.7B's pretrained target leaks 0%, so OPT cells (r1; r5 TV 0.0->0.0, not in pack) cannot show recovery. Targets were never probed, so every target comparison is unprobed vs probed. Harry Potter only; WHP and TV were reapplied by the authors. The appendix grader prompts are the study's own and are not addressed to readers.

statements.correction: After LURK: OPT-2.7B WHP 5.2%, OPT-2.7B TV 0.0% (0.0 before); Llama2-7B WHP 8.4%, TV 4.0%. Range 0–8.4%. Pretrained targets: OPT-2.7B 0.0%, Llama2-7B 32.7%.
statements.problem: The main numbers for this study are all right (WHP 15.5->53.4, 22.7->67.3; TV 29.1->79.7, 45.8->84.9; targets 69.7, 54.6). But the conditions clause 'OPT-2.7B and Llama2-7B stay at 4–8%' leaves out OPT-2.7B TV, which is 0.0% before and after. OPT's pretrained model also leaks 0%.

statements.correction: After LURK: OPT-2.7B WHP 0.0->5.2, TV 0.0->0.0 (target 0.0); Llama2-7B WHP 0.0->8.4, TV 0.04->4.0 (target 32.7). Larger models 53.4–84.9. This study's verdict for the Llama2-7B cells is limits_scope (partial recovery).
statements.problem: '4–8% for OPT-2.7B and Llama2-7B after WHP or TV' is wrong for OPT-2.7B TV (0.0% before and after). OPT's pretrained model leaks 0%, and the authors say probing cannot detect leakage there, so OPT cells are no evidence that recovery fails. Llama2-7B recovers partly (0->8.4, 0.04->4.0, against a 32.7% target): a small rise, which is limits_scope, not the bullet's 'challenges' label.

statements.correction: After LURK: OPT-2.7B 0.0–5.2 (target 0.0); Llama2-7B 4.0–8.4 (target 32.7); Llama2-13B 53.4–79.7 (target 69.7); Llama3.1-8B 67.3–84.9 (target 54.6).
statements.problem: OPT-2.7B TV is 0.0% after LURK, so the small-model range is 0–8.4%, not 4–8%. OPT's low leakage matches its 0% pretrained target (a floor). The size contrast holds for Llama2-7B (target 32.7) against the larger models. Authors: 'Larger LLMs exhibit greater susceptibility to knowledge extraction.'

statements.correction: LURK raises leakage for WHP on Llama3.1-8B from 22.7% to 67.3% (Table 3). WHP was reapplied by the authors, not the released checkpoint.
